entries.title: FAA issues US national ground stop on all flights
entries.summary: The US federal aviation regulator announced a nationwide ground stop for all airports. Federal officials blamed a communications outage and said technicians are investigating.
entries.content:
United States of America

FAA issues US national ground stop on all flights

November 13, 2026

The US federal aviation regulator announced a nationwide ground stop for all airports. Federal officials blamed a communications outage and said technicians are investigating.

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) on Friday issued a ground stop on all national flights. The FAA is the US government agency responsible for air traffic control. 

What do we know so far?

"All departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further notice," the FAA said.

The agency said the ground stop is "due to extraordinary circumstance and reasons for safety." The FAA cited a temporary telecommunication outage and said, "Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis."

The agency later said flights were halted "out of abundance of caution."

In a post on X, US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said the stop was due to a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

"FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them," he wrote.

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that there was no indication this was an attack against the US.

"This is a telecommunications outage," Mullin said. "All the flights are accounted for."

"Everybody's safe. There's no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying," he added.

According to the FlightAware aviation tracker, nearly 7,000 flights in the US were delayed or canceled due to the ground stop.

Canada implementing 'traffic management' measures at major airports

Canada's air navigation service provider, NAV Canada, said it is closely monitoring the US ground stop and later said, "It was implementing traffic management measures at Toronto Pearson, Montreal-Trudeau, Calgary and Vancouver to safely manage traffic volumes."

"Travelers should expect delays and check with their airline. Our systems are operating normally," NAV Canada added.

Toronto Pearson Airport said flights between Toronto and the US have been impacted by the ground stop.

It's the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when the FAA dealt with a system outage. Prior to that, the last ground stop was after the September 11, 2001 terror attacks.

entries.title: Tanker collides with cruise ship on Mississippi in New Orleans
entries.summary: A freighter collided with a cruise ship carrying around 130 people in New Orleans, causing the paddlewheel vessel to capsize. More than 30 people were hospitalized, but all passengers survived and were accounted for.
entries.content:
United States of America

More than 30 hospitalized after cruise ship collision in New Orleans

November 13, 2026

A freighter collided with a cruise ship carrying around 130 people in New Orleans, causing the paddlewheel vessel to capsize. More than 30 people were hospitalized, but all passengers survived and were accounted for.

More than 30 people were hospitalized but no deaths were reported after a freighter collided with a cruise ship on the Mississippi River in the US on Friday. 

Authorities said at least 180 passengers and crew were rescued. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno described it as "a miracle on the Mississippi," adding that none of those hospitalized had critical injuries.

Footage showed the paddlewheel cruise boat, called The American Heritage, capsizing after the impact with the much larger cargo vessel and rescue teams rushing to get people in life jackets out of the water.

'It was just chaos'

The accident happened near the port of New Orleans when the freighter Atlantic Asphalt hit the cruise ship while it was docked.

"It was just chaos," local witness Devon Flanagan was quoted by news agency AP.

"You had all types of ships, like other barges and other companies down there trying to help out, which also was a little convoluted because you had people still in the water," he described the scene.

The company operating The American Heritage , American Cruise Lines, said in a statement that "guests and crew were evacuated, and we are deeply concerned for everyone involved."

According to AP, the cruise ship was built in 2015, is five stories tall and can hold up to 150 passengers. It was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.

When news of the collision broke, it was initially unclear whether there were any fatalities and how many people were injured or missing.

Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry said he was on his way to New Orleans.

"We are aware of the incident on the Mississippi and we are in close contact with local officials and law enforcement," he wrote on X.

US Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote on social media that "we are throwing every asset we have to helping rescue missing passengers" and that his department was coordinating closely with state officials.

entries.title: Ukraine updates: EU to send united front to potential peace talks
entries.summary: Germany, France, the UK, Italy and Poland — as well as the EU itself — will jointly represent Europe in possible peace talks. Meanwhile, a second car bomb in two days has exploded in Moscow. DW has more.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine updates: Europe to send united front to potential peace talks

Published November 13, 2026last updated November 13, 2026

Germany, France, the UK, Italy and Poland — as well as the EU itself — will jointly represent Europe in possible peace talks. Meanwhile, a second car bomb in two days has exploded in Moscow. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The EU has named its representatives to attend possible peace talks between Russia and Ukraine
  • EU foreign policy chief Kallas said Russia does not want 'anybody strong' at the negotiating table
  • The Kremlin said it wants to see 'genuineness' before allowing EU into the talks
  • Germany's Merz called on Trump to make 'no surprises' at his next meeting with Putin

Here are the latest developments from the Russia's war in Ukraine on Friday, November 13: 

Skip next section Russian Foreign Ministry contradicts Kushner on European participation in talks

Russian Foreign Ministry contradicts Kushner on European participation in talks

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova on Friday directly contradicted US envoy Jared Kushner's Thursday statement that President Vladimir Putin had voiced willingness to have European representatives join upcoming talks designed to end his war of aggression against Ukraine.

Responding to a request for comment from Germany's DPA news agency, Zakharova said, "As far as Russia's Foreign Ministry is aware, the issue was not discussed during the talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow."

No Foreign Ministry representatives were present during a Thursday meeting between Putin and US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff according to Russian state media, which said Putin was accompanied by his own foreign policy advisor Yuri Ushakov, Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky and envoy Kirill Dmitriev.

Skip next section Europe to send five-nation team to Russia-Ukraine peace talks

Europe to send five-nation team to Russia-Ukraine peace talks

European Council President Antonio Costa on Friday said the EU will take part in future peace talks aimed at ending Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and will jointly represent Europe with France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK.

"Europe must speak with one clear voice and united voice in all discussion that shape the future of Ukraine and the security of our continent. And this is ultimately a team effort," Costa said after a European leaders' meeting in Dublin.

European and Ukrainian leaders have long insisted on the format, while Russia has rejected the idea and the US appeared indifferent under the Trump administration.

The situation appears to have changed slightly, with US envoy and presidential son-in-law Jared Kushner saying late Thursday, "We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table," adding that Russian President Vladimir Putin "is willing to give it a try."

Despite consensus about wanting peace after nearly five years of Russia's war of aggression, Europe lacks unanimity as to who should be representing the interests of the continent and member states.

Russia and the US have called for one single representative to be present, whereas several nations have called for a diplomatic team.

The question of who will represent the EU itself remains unresolved.

The bloc's foreign affairs boss Kaja Kallas — a staunch critic of Russia and its war — said Friday, "I'm the one who is representing Europe in the foreign and security policy." Adding, "I know that the Russians don’t want me, but, you know, do we have a say, who is representing Russia?"

With frustration growing over Russian aggression on Europe's doorstep, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs put things in perspective. Pointing to the fact that Europe is more populous, richer and more militarily powerful than Russia, he said Friday, "We as Europe, have to grow some bigger balls."

Skip next section Zelenskyy says 'no clear explanations given' for the Starshield speed issues

Zelenskyy says 'no clear explanations given' for the Starshield speed issues

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said no clear explanations have been given for recent speed issues with Starshield.

The Ukrainian president said on Thursday that Ukraine's military faced new "systematic restrictions" to tech billionaire Elon Musk's Starshield satellite internet.

Zelenskyy doubled down on his comments on Friday, saying the issue remained unsolved.

He said the connections were only working when devices were moving slower than 161 kilometres (100 miles) per hour.

"This makes it impossible, in particular, to use interceptors against jet-powered 'Shaheds.'" he added. The Ukrainian president also said he instructed his ministers to step up contacts with the US side.

The Starshield military communications system — the military-grade version of satellite-based communication network Starlink — is operated by Musk's SpaceX and plays a key role for frontline communications.

Ukraine first flagged issues with Starshield last month after a dispute between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump over a US deal allowing more Russian diesel into global markets.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk "capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network."

Tech billionaire and US president both denied throttling Ukrainian access, but Musk later accused Ukraine of using the service for military purposes while Trump said Musk had "put it back."

Skip next section Merz asks Trump for 'no surprises' at Putin meeting

Merz asks Trump for 'no surprises' at Putin meeting

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday asked US President Donald Trump to not make any "surprises" on Ukraine with the Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump is expected to meet with Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at an APEC leaders' summit in China next week.

Speaking on the sidelines of the European Union meetings in Dublin, Merz said that "some here ⁠in ⁠fear this could turn into a 'second Anchorage moment'."

The Russian and US presidents held talks in Anchorage, Alaska, last summer, the outcome of which European side views as favoring Putin.

"I ‌therefore want to state our message to the United States very clearly: Please, no surprises. Continue to ‌play as part of 'Team Europe' and 'Team Ukraine'," Merz said.

He also stated that Europe does not need to talk about security arrangements with Russia.

"Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that, it already exists," he said.

Merz also said it was a "given" that his country would involved in the next round of Ukraine talks.

Skip next section WATCH: As Russia pounds Ukraine's infrastructure, Kyiv faces winter blackouts

WATCH: As Russia pounds Ukraine's infrastructure, Kyiv faces winter blackouts

Kyiv residents are bracing for another difficult winter as Russian airstrikes continue to target the Ukrainian capital’s energy infrastructure. Long and unpredictable power and water outages are disrupting daily life, forcing families to rely on batteries, portable power stations and improvised routines.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: EU leaders tussle over whom to send to Ukraine, Russia peace talks

IN DEPTH: EU leaders tussle over whom to send to Ukraine, Russia peace talks

European leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the Europeans will be present at the next meetings.

When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.

The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi, followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

The pair then hot-footed their way to Dublin to debrief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelekenskyy.

Zelenskyy and Kushner also said Thursday that Europeans would be at the table for the next talks with Russia on ending the war.

Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine, alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa. As yet, the EU hasn’t been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.

Read more about the uncertainty over Europe’s representation in the Ukraine peace talks

Skip next section Russia says it wants to 'understand Europe's genuine intention' before allowing EU into talks

Russia says it wants to 'understand Europe's genuine intention' before allowing EU into talks

Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Russia needs clarity on the European Union's "real intentions" for joining the Ukraine peace talks before making a decision on whether to expand the trilateral format.

US negotiators ‌said on Thursday that ‌President ​Vladimir Putin had agreed to an EU seat at the table, but Peskov's remarks indicate that the Kremlin has not yet agreed.

"Once we understand their real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format," Peskov said.

"If the Europeans really do have someone who is at least authorized in some way to talk, and if the Europeans really do have the desire to do so, then, of course, we will be ready to talk to them," he said.

Speaking after the latest trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday, Russia's lead negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, claimed that "Russia did not receive single concrete peace proposal from European countries."

Skip next section EU top diplomat: Russia does not want someone strong on the other side

EU top diplomat: Russia does not want someone strong on the other side

The European Union (EU) foreign affairs chief, Kaja Kallas, said Russia did not want ​"anybody strong" at the negotiating table because "they ​want to ​push through their maximum ​demands."

Arriving at an EU summit in Dublin, Kallas told reporters that Moscow had no say over who represented the European Union in the US-mediated Ukraine-Russia peace talks.

"First we need a ceasefire. If we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us, which is that we divert the attention away from that there is no ceasefire," she said.

EU leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent the European Union in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the bloc will be present at the next meetings.

Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war in Ukraine, alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa.

As yet, the EU hasn't been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.

Skip next section Ukraine and Russia exchange drone attacks overnight

Ukraine and Russia exchange drone attacks overnight

Overnight drone attacks killed several people in both Ukraine and Russia.

In the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa, authorities said two people had been killed and five others injured. One person was reportedly injured in an attack on a hospital, according to reports from the capital city of Kyiv.

A Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia in the southeast killed a 17-year-old boy, acting regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said.

Meanwhile, In the Russian city of Volgograd, four people were killed and two others injured, regional government said.

Skip next section Car bomb wounded an aide to former pro-Russia Ukrainian prime minister — reports

Car bomb wounded an aide to former pro-Russia Ukrainian prime minister — reports

Russia's Investigative Committee has launched an inquiry into the explosion of a car belonging to an exiled Ukrainian political aide in Moscow, media reported.

The car reportedly belonged to Sergei Zavorotniy, a former spokesman for Mykola Azarov, who served as Ukraine's prime minister from 2010 to 2014. He fled to Russia from Ukraine amid anti-government protests in 2014.

According to the Russian newspaper Kommersant, Zavorotniy was hospitalized. Both Ren TV and the 112 Telegram channel reported that he lost his left arm in the attack and sustained a concussion, rib fractures, and other injuries.

Meanwhile, Azarov told Russia's TASS state news agency on Friday that he does not know anything about the explosion except that Zavorotniy survived.

This is the second reported car explosion in Russia following the death of a Russian serviceman in a car explosion in Saint Petersburg on Thursday.

There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

EU leaders are set to convene in the Irish capital, Dublin, for an informal European Council meeting on Friday. They are under pressure to nominate someone to represent the European Union in the Ukraine peace talks.

In other news, a car bomb exploded in Russia, targeting a former aide to the pro-Russia Ukrainian politician Mykola Azarov.

Follow along for the latest updates on the peace talks and other news from Ukraine.

entries.title: David Walliams: UK police launch sex offense probe into comedian
entries.summary: The "Little Britain" star and "Britain's Got Talent" judge has been accused of engaging in sexual misconduct and inappropriate behavior towards young women and girls. Walliams denies the allegations.
entries.content:
November 13, 2026

The "Little Britain" star and "Britain's Got Talent" judge has been accused of engaging in sexual misconduct and inappropriate behavior towards young women and girls. Walliams denies the allegations.

London police on Friday said they are opening an sexual offenses investigation into British actor, comedian and children's author David Walliams.

The Metropolitan Police said they "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offenses involving a man now in his 50s."

It comes after British outlets ITV News and The Guardian paper reported that Walliams misused his power and celebrity status to prey on women and girls over a period of more than 20 years. The media outlets produced an hourlong video documentary on the allegations against Walliams, entitled "David Walliams: Power and Silence."

The documentary reported on a woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Walliams when she was 15. The outlets also highlighted sexual harassment and inappropriate conduct allegations regarding "Britain's Got Talent," where he was a judge, and his book publisher HarperCollins.

"We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offense to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened," said Detective Mike Cagney, who is in charge of the Met Police investigation.

The Met Police investigation is based on allegations against Walliams that are separate from those reported by the two news outlets.

Walliams denies allegations

Neither Walliams nor his lawyer have responded to the Met Police investigation. However, Walliams did respond earlier to the ITV and Guardian report about him.

"I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me," Walliams told the outlets in a letter. "Whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something I never did."

The allegations against Walliams have already have already had repercussions on his career. The BBC took down content featuring Walliams from its platforms, including comedy sketch show "Little Britain."

Walliams' publisher, HarperCollins UK, dropped him last year after The Telegraph newspaper reported on inappropriate behavior towards women at the publishing firm.

UK media and entertainment industry faces sexual abuse reckoning

The allegations come as several male comedic and literary figures in the UK have faced either sexual assault charges or accusations in recent years.

Media personality and actor Russell Brand on Monday was sentenced to 10 years and 6 months imprisonment after he was convicted of rape and assault.

In 2024, children's book author Neil Gaiman was accused of sexual assault, leading companies such as Disney and DC Comics to drop adaptations of his works. Gaiman denies the allegations.

"The media industry will need to look at itself and ensure whether it is taking all of the steps needed to protect the safety of woman and girls who work within the industry," British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Thursday.

British Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy is expected to meet with entertainment industry leaders next week, where she will deliver a warning that the UK government could intervene if they do not protect those who blow the whistle on sexual assault and misconduct.

entries.title: Pope Leo celebrates Mass in his former diocese of Chiclayo, Peru
entries.summary: Over a million people have gathered for Mass with Pope Leo XIV on Friday. The event in northern Peru, where he served as bishop before becoming head of the Catholic Church, is the centerpiece of his South American tour.
entries.content:
Peru

Pope Leo celebrates Mass in his former diocese of Chiclayo, Peru

November 13, 2026

Over a million people have gathered for Mass with Pope Leo XIV on Friday. The event in northern Peru, where he served as bishop before becoming head of the Catholic Church, is the centerpiece of his South American tour.

Pope Leo XIV was greeted by another enormous crowd on Friday as he arrived at Pampas de Pimentel, a vast desert park outside the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo, to celebrate an outdoor Mass in a diocese that he served as bishop for eight years before being summoned to Rome in 2023, where he was later elected pontiff.

The Vatican estimates that roughly 1.5 million faithful braved scorching sun and heat of 31 degrees Celsius (87 degrees Fahrenheit) to attend.

The event was the centerpiece of Leo's 12-day South American tour, throughout which an estimated 12 million people have turned out at stops in Uruguay and Argentina and now Peru.

'Padre Roberto' returns home as 'Papa Leon'

Pope Leo, born Robert Prevost in Chicago, Illinois, had already referred to Peru, where he served as a missionary for some 20 years, as his homeland in remarks delivered on Wednesday.

Beyond US and Vatican citizenship, Leo also holds a Peruvian passport.

Leo, whom locals still refer to as "Padre Roberto" and "amigo," arrived from the capital Lima on Friday morning in a plane adorned with stickers reading "Leo XIV flies home." The leader of the Catholic Church's 1.4 billion members will remain in Chiclayo until Sunday.

An agricultural and commercial hub on the Pacific coast, Chiclayo is Peru's fourth largest city and has a population of 700,000. Beyond locals, many of those attending Mass on Friday told reporters that they had journeyed from far-flung regions and even neighboring countries to receive the pope's blessing.

The crowds that Leo has attracted throughout his trip, undertaken shortly after he underwent surgery for lung cancer in Rome, have grown along the way, with the largest gathering coming in Lima on Wednesday, where an estimated 3.5 million people turned out.

Pope overwhelmed with emotion, thanks Chiclayo faithful for their prayers

Though normally reserved, Leo has openly displayed his emotions since returning to Peru — laughing, singing and tearing up while interacting with crowds of faithful both young and old.

After making his way through the massive crowd to celebrate Mass on Friday, Leo began his sermon with words of thanks.

"What a joy it is to return to Chiclayo!" Leo said at the start of his homily, "It is a blessing for me to be with you once again."

"As I look your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life."

"Thank you for your affection, support and prayers, especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming," Leo told the crowd.

Pope Leo will deliver remarks at university named for role-model missionary

On Friday afternoon, the pontiff will deliver a speech at Chiclayo's St. Turibius de Mogrovejo Catholic University, where he once served as chancellor.

The institution is named after a sixteenth century Spanish missionary who would become the first archbishop of Lima. He served as a role model for Leo during his own ministry.

Mogrovejo was known to travel long distances on horseback to spread the gospel, as well as for standing up for the rights of indigenous and enslaved peoples.

Leo, too, is remembered for his outreach and for championing human rights and social justice, especially for the poor.

entries.title: The dangers of revising Europe's security architecture
entries.summary: Experts warn against revising Europe's security framework because they say it would mean granting Moscow its longstanding wish of renegotiating postwar security on the continent.
entries.content:
Ukraine

The dangers of revising Europe's security architecture

November 13, 2026

Experts warn against revising Europe's security framework because they say it would mean granting Moscow its longstanding wish of renegotiating postwar security on the continent.

European leaders have so far found compromises in response to many of US President Donald Trump's demands.

But they were surprised to hear Trump say that he raised Europe's security framework with Russian officials.

"It's going to be a big agreement and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House last week.

He said that deal might include all of Europe. But what he meant by "all of Europe" was not clear.

US envoy Jared Kushner also wrote that Europe and Russia had struggled to establish a sustainable security framework for more than 30 years.

Kushner said he was looking at a "broader" European architecture before he flew to meet with Russian and Ukrainian representatives in Abu Dhabi.

European diplomats immediately pushed back on Washington's approach to secure a peace deal in Ukraine because they feared that a peace settlement could restore Russia's sphere of influence and undermine NATO.

"We ​already have European security ​architecture in place. NATO and the European Union both have their ​respective roles. We ​must make sure Ukraine is integrated ‌into ⁠this architecture," said Kaja Kallas, the European Union's foreign policy chief.

The issue with revising Europe's postwar security framework

Russia made clear during talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week that they were keen to discuss a broader European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.

"Phrases about the European security architecture are certainly Russian talking points and not only talking points but, to a degree, part of a media propaganda effort that Russia makes to frame the war as it wishes to frame the war," said Michael Kimmage, a historian of the Cold War.

Russian leaders, including Vladimir Putin, have long alleged that the US and NATO repeatedly violated pledges they made in the early 1990s not to expand the alliance into the former Soviet bloc.

They have seen NATO's enlargement during this period as having put them in a humiliating position in which they could do very little.

At the same time, in the 1990s, the European project saw the birth of the European Union, the single market that ensured the free movement of goods and people across member states, the Schengen agreement for border-free travel, and the euro.

The core idea was to extend peace across the continent.

"Europe can mean so many things, but the European project was not designed for war. It was designed for peace," said Kimmage.

During this period, there were even suggestions of Russia becoming a NATO member.

But that relative period of stability changed after Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Russia wants to redraw all of this by force. And I think that that's fundamentally unacceptable to Europe with all the diversity and variations that you get within the European landscape on what's acceptable and not acceptable. I think the large-scale redrawing of borders by force is just not the European project," said Kimmage.

"So to the extent that the redrawing of borders by force is the lifeblood of Russian foreign policy, and I think that's a pretty easy case to make, Russia and Europe are at an impasse," he said.

What was to happen to Ukraine's security?

The Trump administration very quickly turned to making sure that "existing European security institutions" would be intact, with Jared Kushner having said late Thursday that the next round of negotiations would include "our European partners."

Kushner, along with Steve Witkoff, flew to Moscow to talk to Putin after talks in Abu Dhabi. Then they flew to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Kushner had earlier Thursday signaled some "really incredible" postwar plans for Ukraine, saying that it could not be concluded without Europeans at the table.

"We should not allow a diktat from Russia that would result in some kind of neutralization or significant reduction in the military forces of Ukraine going forward, because that would make Ukraine very, very vulnerable to future aggression and pressure coming from Russia," said Hiski Haukkala, the director of the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.

That would mean that Ukraine would also be completely dependent on the security guarantees that the US or Europeans are able and willing to provide.

"We are supporting Ukraine because we are supporting international law and the basic norms of decency and international security when it comes to European security architecture. And this is the vantage point from which we are operating," he said.

The European Union has repeatedly pointed to some of the basic treaties that Russia broke, including:

  • The UN Charter
  • The Helsinki Act of 1975, which established the ten core principles of European security, including the non-use of force or threat against territorial integrity.
  • The Charter of Paris for a New Europe that built on Helsinki commitments
  • The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), which was one of the few multilateral security forums where the West and Russia engaged.
  • The Budapest Memorandum of 1994 in which Russia, the US and the UK provided security assurances to Ukraine and others in exchange for them giving up their nuclear weapons.

"Russia walked away from these principles and smashed them to pieces in the process. And they are not interested in reinstating the previous security architecture order. They want something different in its stead. And as long as this is not on the table, the Russian form of negotiation is to wage war. War is a form of bargaining," Haukkala said.

"And they are signaling strategic intent to change the makeup of European security, to subdue Ukraine and to change the very essence of European security," he added.

What is the way forward?

Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for European Affairs in the George W. Bush administration, said Russia is very good at sticking to its demands.

He said Russians know how to negotiate and "right now, they are not negotiating," referring to talks in Abu Dhabi.

Some experts said there was no possibility of having a new security architecture with the Russians at this point because there was no trust or common vision to align with Russia at the moment.

Others like Balazs Jarabik, an expert on post-Soviet politics, said that Russia was part of the European security architecture whether Europeans liked it or not.

"And the question is whether it's included as our enemy. Obviously, Russia is not going to be a partner, right? We have to find a modus operandi to reduce the risk of a horizontal escalation and potentially a bigger European war, even a bigger one than what we have now."

A host of European leaders on Friday rejected the Russian demands to discuss Europe's security framework as well, with a spokesperson for the German government saying that Berlin was looking to host a meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" to secure funding for Ukraine's defense and reach a unified position regarding future peace talks.

entries.title: EU leaders urged to 'act now' to stay AI competitive with US, China
entries.summary: EU leaders in Dublin were called on by an AI executive to move quickly in the tech race with the US and China. EU official Metsola, however, expressed frustration with the idea that the bloc is behind in AI development.
entries.content:
Published November 13, 2026last updated November 13, 2026

EU leaders in Dublin were called on by an AI executive to move quickly in the tech race with the US and China. EU official Metsola, however, expressed frustration with the idea that the bloc is behind in AI development.

European Union leaders met in Dublin on Friday at the first ever summit on artificial intelligence (AI). The meeting came at a critical moment, as the bloc seeks a unified policy on the rapidly evolving technology.

The meeting took place in Dublin's Convention Center, which was also the meeting place of the European Political Community summit this week.

Mistral's CEO Mensch urges EU to 'act now'

French AI company Mistral's CEO Arthur Mensch, as well as Nobel-prize winner and researcher Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the "godfather of AI," spoke to EU leaders at the summit.

"Europe has all the technology and the talent to lead the AI race," Mensch said during the event. "What it needs is speed, financing and a strong coordination between member states."

Mensch urged the leaders to "act now" to stay competitive with the US and China in regards to AI development.

"AI is the most important technology of our time," European Council ‌President Antonio Costa said in a post on X regarding the summit. "Europe must make the most of its benefits, from higher productivity to better public services. We must also manage the risks and changes it will bring — and help set global standards for responsible governance and safe, human-centric AI."

The summit took place at a time of mounting worries about the emerging technology, which promises to transform ‌industries, labor markets and societies.

It also came in the wake of a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents in recent months and the wider discussion about how the technology could harm humanity.

Tech leaders behind the technology have also fallen under scrutiny. As recently as this week, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was forced to resign after it was revealed that he had been in a relationship with a Chinese spy and a direct report in his company.

Finding Europe's role in the AI revolution

During the summit, a discussion occurred about where Europe fits in within the AI movement.

European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said she frustrated with the notion that Europe had "somehow lost the AI race."

She noted that the EU has "world-class talent, technological expertise and industrial experience to lead in AI."

"What we need now is to ensure that our ideas have the financing they need to grow and succeed in Europe," she added.

EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said there is a "dark side" to AI.

"We can all already see this in the battlefield in Ukraine, where you have drones equipped by artificial intelligence to really train to find anybody to kill," Kallas, the former prime minister of Estonia, said at the event.

Leaders face questions on how to unlock AI's potential, how to catch up with China and the United States in the race for the technology, but also how to protect against the risks it poses to individuals and businesses.

The governments of Estonia and Finland wrote in a letter ahead of the summit that Europe must "establish EU-level arrangements for responding to serious AI incidents," calling for "developing advanced AI and governing it responsibly."

entries.title: What's going on with the polar vortex?
entries.summary: Observations show the ring of fierce winds that rotate at the Earth's North Pole has changed direction. Scientists say it's a historic disruption and the earliest reversal on record. What could it mean for the weather?
entries.content:
Nature and EnvironmentGlobal issues

Earliest polar vortex on record arrives: What does it mean for winter?

November 13, 2026

Observations show the ring of fierce winds that rotate at the Earth's North Pole has changed direction. Scientists say it's a historic disruption and the earliest reversal on record. What could it mean for the weather?

High up in the atmosphere, there's a ring of cold air swirling over the Arctic that can intensify, weaken, and shapeshift through the seasons. This is the polar vortex.

If it gets disrupted, this twisting pool of chilly air can influence the weather we experience, increasing the risk of a cold snap in the Northern Hemisphere. 

Current observations show the vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with its winds reversing directions.

Earliest vortex disruption on record

It's not yet clear how the current disruption to the polar vortex will affect the Northern Hemisphere winter, but scientists agree it is a record-breaking event.

"As far as we know, this is the earliest stratospheric vortex disruption that has been observed," European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast (ECMWF) principal scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart told the AFP news agency.

The French meteorological agency Meteo-France, meanwhile, called it "an unprecedented event."

The early breakdown of the vortex "really increases the chance of cold air outbreaks across the latitudes where most of the densely populated population centers are across the Northern Hemisphere, US, Europe and East Asia," Judah Cohen, a climatologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology told AFP.

What exactly is the polar vortex and how does it work?

The polar vortex is an enormous band of cold, low-pressure air that spins counterclockwise around the North Pole, about 10 to 50 kilometers (around 6 to 30 miles) above the surface.

It's closely connected to the jet stream, another band of powerful winds just below the vortex. The jet stream forms a boundary where the cold Arctic air meets warmer air from the tropics and subtropics.

The vortex can sometimes be a tight circle, keeping the coldest air locked around the North Pole over winter. It can also form uneven waves that dip southwards. And as it changes in strength and shape, that can influence the atmosphere below and alter the position of the jet stream, which drives the weather on the ground.

So, if the jet stream is more "wavy," and plunges south, it may also allow freezing Arctic air to spill southward.

One of the biggest influences that can provoke this kind of disruption is known as "sudden stratospheric warming." This is when temperatures in the polar stratosphere rise dramatically within a few days, causing the vortex's strong westerly winds to weaken.

This can push the vortex off its spot at the North Pole, make it split apart into multiple rings, or — as is happening now — cause the westerly winds to change direction.

It can take several weeks for the vortex to recover.

What does this mean for winter weather?

A previous polar vortex disruption contributed to the deadly Great Texas Freeze in February 2021, which caused more than a week of freezing temperatures that sparked power outages and killed hundreds of people.

But bone-chilling cold isn't a foregone conclusion. The Met Office, which is the UK's national weather and climate service, stresses that what's happening with the polar vortex can nudge odds in that direction, but it's not a switch that turns cold weather on and off.

Other weather patterns can also influence the outcome.

For example, there's a possibility El Nino, which is associated with milder winters, could "moderate or modify" the impacts, Cohen told AFP. But he added this was not certain. 

The El Nino weather phenomenon, caused by the warming of surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is currently intensifying and is expected to peak at the end of the year. The ongoing event has been classified as exceptionally strong and is disrupting weather around the globe.

Some research has also linked the rapid warming of the Arctic driven by climate change to increasing disruptions to the polar vortex. That means that, even as the planet warms, some areas may still experience more severe cold spells. But this connection is not conclusive and is still debated by scientists.

entries.title: Ice hockey: Russia threatens against Canada and Germany over exclusion from tournaments
entries.summary: A fortnight after the CAS ordered ice hockey's governing body to reintegrate Russia into international play, a solution remains elusive. Now Russia has threatened to take legal action against two tournament hosts.
entries.content:
November 13, 2026

A fortnight after the CAS ordered ice hockey's governing body to reintegrate Russia into international play, a solution remains elusive. Now Russia has threatened to take legal action against two tournament hosts.

"Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.

"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak added after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.

"The IIHF as a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, don't hold it at all, or impose sanctions on Canada."

Canada refuses to bend on junior tournament

The threat comes after the Canadian government confirmed on Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to play in the IIHF World Junior Championship starting on December 26 in Alberta.

"Canada's position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues ⁠its war of aggression ​against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual," Canadian Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden said in a statement. "Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine."

Following last month's Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling, in which it said that the security concerns the IIHF cited for barring Russian teams from taking part in international tournaments was not sufficient – the world governing body pledged to work to comply with the decision.

Norway then said it had been bumped from the World Juniors and had been informed by the IIHF that Russia would take its place. Several other national hockey associations said they had received a revised schedule for the tournament and stated that they would not play against Russia. The IIHF has not confirmed the change.

Men's tournament with Russia 'effectively impossible'

Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and host nation Canada closely, as it is set to host the IIHF World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf starting on May 14. With several nations saying they will not play Russia and major sponsors threatening to pull out, a German government spokesman described the prospect of hosting the tournament under these conditions as "effectively impossible."

However, Germany has ruled out taking the Canadian approach.

Ronald Rauhe, Germany's minister of state for sport said on Wednesday that refusing to grant visas was "not a solution for the (German) ice hockey federation (DEB), nor is it a solution for successfully hosting a World Championship anywhere."

At the same time, though, he expressed support for the DEB in its wish to host the tournament as planned.

"We believe that we should channel all our energy and efforts into helping sport—and ice hockey in particular—find a solution, which would, of course, entail excluding Russia from the World Championship."

Munich's Olympic bid and the IOC's new stance on Russia

What makes things even more complicated for German officials are concerns that taking a hardline on Russia could jeopardize Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees bidding to host an Olympic Games to follow its lead. The IOC is set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process.

For now, though, the ball appears to be in the IIHF's court, after Ottawa confirmed its refusal to grant Russians visas to play in the World Juniors. How the dispute regarding that tournament gets resolved could go a long way to pointing the way forward for the men's tournament in Germany next May.

entries.title: Why does El Salvador's Bukele have troops in Haiti?
entries.summary: Haiti's Prime Minister congratulating El Salvador's President for a gang crackdown in Haiti has shone a light on the relationship between the two countries. What's going on, and where does the US stand?
entries.content:
Haiti

Why does El Salvador have troops in Haiti?

November 13, 2026

Haiti's Prime Minister congratulating El Salvador's President for a gang crackdown in Haiti has shone a light on the relationship between the two countries. What's going on, and where does the US stand?

Haiti has been engulfed in crisis since 2018, with protests, a presidential assassination and widespread gang violence bringing the country to its knees.

But earlier this week, Haiti's Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime hailed a major win in the battle against the violence, thanks to "the commitment of the Salvadorean forces in the fight against gangs."

El Salvador's President, Nayib Bukele had earlier said a joint task force between the countries had "destroyed" what he called "the house of Lanmo San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters." He also tweeted out an as-yet unverified video of helicopters firing on a sprawling property.

Why are troops from El Salvador in Haiti?

A number of Salvadoran troops have been stationed in Haiti, nearly 2,000 kilometers from their homeland, since the beginning of 2025, mostly in an attempt to curb gang influence.

Last month, Bukele dispatched more than 2,000 troops and special forces to Haiti, ostensibly to rescue four Salvadorans who were ambushed on October 18 and have not yet been found.

Writing on social media platform X, Fils-Aime thanked the Salvadorean military for helping "the fight against gangs." The two nations are, he added, working alongside the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), in an attempt to "regain control of the territory and restore state authority."

The GSF has been operating in Haiti since 2016. But there are doubts to the legitimacy of El Salvador's presence.

"Where the lines are and where the coordination begins and ends between a bunch of distinct entities and security forces is a huge concern about how this actually plays out, and El Salvador are trying to frame it as their choice, their action," Jake Johnston, a Haiti expert and director of international research at the Center for Economic and Policy Research (CEPR) in Washington, told non-profit news agency The New Humanitarian this week.

What is the current situation in Haiti?

 A UN report about Haiti released on Thursday described "bloody turf wars, sexual violence and other horrors, noting that serious violations and abuses continue to be committed across the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area and in the Artibonite and South-East departments."

It further found that between July and September 2026, at least 1,167 people were killed and 459 injured, with more than half of that violence stemming from "ground or aerial operations carried out by security forces against gangs, sometimes with the support of a private military company using drones."

For many observers, this chaos is a major part of the appeal for Bukele, who appears to wish to export his mano dura (iron fist) policy on to foreign soil. The policy saw gang members jailed on a huge scale and a significant drop in the murder rate of a country once notorious for homicide. But Romain Le Cour Grandmaison, a Haiti expert from the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, told DW earlier this month that Haiti's gang problem is more entrenched. He says using the same tactics as in El Salvador may not have the same result.

"Haiti does not currently have the conditions to replicate the Salvadoran model: Its prisons were emptied in 2024, its justice system is largely paralyzed and criminal groups resemble militias more than gangs, with territory, taxes, weapons of war and political networks that protect them," Le Cour Grandmaison said.

Does El Salvador have US support?

Despite El Salvador being on Donald Trump's list of "shithole countries" that the US president disparaged in 2018 in notorious remarks which he later partially denied, relations between the US and El Salvador have improved markedly during Trump's second term.

The number of migrants deported to El Salvador from the US rose by 98% at the start of 2026 and Le Cour Grandmaison said the US plays "a central, albeit very discreet, role in public life" in El Salvador.

Bukele's move to position himself as an ally of Trump has seen the US president offer him a level of endorsement and autonomy to do what Bukele deems necessary to protect El Salvador's security and that of its troops.

"He said that he has a big problem with Haiti. I said: 'Look, you're running your country. You have to do what you have to do,'" Trump said in November.
